yaml.title: Phenological Changes in Pollination Pals
yaml.author: Aubrey Monaco
yaml.subtitle: Synchrony Shifts in the Ruby-throated Hummingbird and Preferred Flowers

markdown.markdown: With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, migrating birds are starting to move back to their breeding grounds earlier each year [@gill2014]. Along with this, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (*Archilochus colubris*), feed on may be changing their flowering times due to climate change [@xie2025]. ![[Ruby-throated Hummingbird]{style="color:darkblue;"}[@ruby-thr2024]](data/rth_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="400"} I want to investigate how the Ruby-throated Hummingbird has been shifting its spring migration patterns at varying latitudes, based on Courter et al., 2013 [@courter2013], and how the appearances of two spring ephemeral species it prefers to feed on during this migration, Red Buckeye (*Aesculus pavia*) and Red Columbine (*Aquilegia canadensis*), has changed (or not changed) over the past 10\* years, also at varying latitudes [@ruby-thra]. \*My maps and graphs are from 2014 to 2025 to account for any incomplete datasets from 2025 ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ![[Red Columbine]{style="color:darkred;"} [@wildcola]](data/cb_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="200"} ![[Red Buckeye]{style="color:darkred;"} [@redbucka]](data/rb_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="226"} ::: I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back to their breeding grounds earlier each year, and that they are arriving at higher latitudes increasingly earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of Red Columbine and Red Buckeye will be earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes compared to previous years. So, as Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate back earlier, these flowers may not be available at lower latitudes for them to feed on. # Materials and Methods ::: panel-tabset ## 1. ### Install Packages and Load Libraries ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE #install.packages("leaflet") # Dynamic maps #install.packages("leaflet.providers") # Different Basemaps #install.packages("leaflet.extras") # Heatmaps #install.packages("rinat") # Downloads iNaturalist data #install.packages("rnpn") # Downloads US National Phenology Network Data #install.packages("plotly") # Interactive graphs library(doParallel) # Download data in a parallel loop library(foreach) # Download data in a loop library(plotly) library(leaflet) library(leaflet.providers) library(leaflet.extras) library(rinat) library(rnpn) library(knitr) # Making tables library(rvest) # Used to download data from Journey North library(dplyr) # Mutating and filtering data library(lubridate) # Parsing date data library(tidyr) # Cleaning data library(ggplot2)# Plotting trends ``` ## 2. ### Flowers: Load iNaturalist and US NPN Data. - foreach, doParallel, and rinat package iNaturalist data download: - taxon_name is set to each desired species, place_id is set to 1 for the United States, maxresults is set to 10000 to ensure all data is downloaded, and quality is set to "research" to ensure verified data ```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE # Registering cores for downloading data num_cores <- parallel::detectCores() - 1 registerDoParallel(num_cores) # Parallel data download for both species 2005-2019 (Works because there is a smaller amount of data) nat_0519 <- foreach(s = c("Aesculus pavia", "Aquilegia canadensis"), .packages = c("dplyr", "rinat"), .errorhandling = "pass", .combine = bind_rows) %:% foreach(a = c(2005:2019), .packages = c("dplyr", "rinat"), .combine = bind_rows) %dopar% { print(paste("Downloading data for year:", a)) Sys.sleep(60) get_inat_obs(taxon_name = s, year = a, place_id = 1, maxresults = 10000, quality = "research") } # Sequential data download for both species 2020-2025 (Sequential was needed for the larger amount of data) nat_2025 <- foreach(s = c("Aesculus pavia", "Aquilegia canadensis"), .packages = c("dplyr", "rinat"), .combine = rbind) %:% foreach(a = c(2020:2025), .packages = c("dplyr", "rinat"), .combine = rbind) %do% { print(paste("Downloading data for year:", a)) Sys.sleep(60) get_inat_obs(taxon_name = s, year = a, place_id = 1, maxresults = 10000, quality = "research") } ``` - Individual datasets combined and written csv is loaded into environment as "nat_flower": ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE #fl_all <- rbind(nat_0519, nat_2025) Commented out after running once #write.csv(fl_all, "data/fl_all.csv") Commented out after running once nat_flower <- read.csv("data/fl_all.csv") nat_flower <- nat_flower %>% filter(common_name %in% c("red columbine", "Red Buckeye")) %>% # Removed other species that got lumped in with the download mutate(year = year(observed_on)) %>% # Pulling year from date mutate(observed_on = as.character(observed_on)) # Reformatting for joining ``` - rnpn package for NPN data download (automatically saves as a csv): ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE # Species IDs are available through the NPN's website (Red Buckeye = 784, Red Columbine = 147) npn_download_individual_phenometrics( request_source='Aubrey Monaco', years=c(2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025), species_id=c(784, 147), download_path="data/npn_flower.csv" ) ``` - NPN data loaded into environment: ```{r} #| code-fold: TRUE npn_flower <- read.csv("data/npn_flower.csv") npn_flower <- npn_flower %>% mutate(observed_on = make_date(year = last_yes_year, month = last_yes_month, day = last_yes_day)) %>% # Creating matching column to iNat data for joining mutate(observed_on = as.character(observed_on)) ``` ## 3. ### Flowers: Combine the iNaturalist and NPN Data ```{r, message=FALSE} # iNaturalist (~50,000 points) and NPN (~7,000 points) data are joined by common values, and non-matching observations are kept; Duplicate observations are removed, leaving about 52,000 data points all_flower <- nat_flower %>% full_join(npn_flower) all_flower <- all_flower[!duplicated(as.list(all_flower))] all_flower <- all_flower %>% distinct() ``` ## 4. ### Flowers: Standardize and Mutate Data ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} # dplyr and lubridate used to standardize and add columns from dates all_flower <- all_flower %>% mutate(observed_on = parse_date_time(observed_on, orders = c("mdy", "ydm", "dmy"))) %>% # Standardizes date formats mutate(year = year(observed_on)) %>% mutate(year_day = yday(observed_on)) %>% # Puts date into day out of 365 mutate(month = month(observed_on)) # Pulls month from date ``` ## 5. ### Flowers: Calculate Means of Early Period (2005-2013) - Found the mean date of first flower sightings from 2005 to 2013 and from March to May (when these flowers' bloom times overlap) [@redcolu2004a; @usdaplab] - Separated sightings into 3 bands of latitude to account for difference in average flowering times across their range (grouped by latitudes with similar "year_day" averages) ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE fl_early <- all_flower %>% filter(year %in% c(2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013) & month %in% c(3, 4, 5)) fl_early_all <- fl_early %>% mutate(latbin=cut(latitude, breaks = c(30,36,42,48), labels = c("30-36", "36-42", "42-48"))) %>% group_by(latbin) %>% mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm=TRUE)) fl_means <- fl_early_all %>% group_by(latbin) %>% summarise(mean) %>% rename("Latitude" = "latbin", "Flowering Day Mean" = "mean") # One row for each latitude band mean selected selected_fl <- fl_means[c(1, 25, 68), ] # Converting yearday into date (DOYs taken from "mean" column of fl_early_all) origin_date <- as.Date(paste0(2013, "-01-01")) fl_early_date1 <- as.Date(82 - 1, origin = origin_date) fl_early_date2 <- as.Date(98 - 1, origin = origin_date) fl_early_date3 <- as.Date(108 - 1, origin = origin_date) fl_early_dates <- c(fl_early_date1, fl_early_date2, fl_early_date3) fl_early_dates <- format(fl_early_dates, format = "%B %d") selected_fl <- cbind(selected_fl, fl_early_dates) selected_fl <- selected_fl %>% rename("Flowering Date" = "...3") # Table to show early period flowering times based on latitude bands kable(selected_fl, format = "pipe", caption = '2005-2013 Flowering Time Means (days)', align = "c") ``` ## 6. ### Flowers: Calculate Means and Difference From 2014-2025 to 2005-2013 - Added a column (mean0513) based on "2005-2013 Flowering Time Means" table and assigned by corresponding latitudes - Used 6 bands of latitude for more specific analysis - Created a "difference" column, showing the difference in days of arrival between the early and current average using mean - mean0513 - Bound all of these bands into one dataset for plotting ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE fl_new <- all_flower %>% filter(year %in% c(2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) & month %in% c(3, 4, 5)) %>% mutate(mean0513 = case_when( latitude > 30 & latitude < 33 ~ 81.95652, latitude > 33 & latitude < 36 ~ 81.95652, latitude > 36 & latitude < 39 ~ 98.34783, latitude > 39 & latitude < 42 ~ 98.34783, latitude > 42 & latitude < 45 ~ 107.73913, latitude > 45 & latitude < 48 ~ 107.73913)) fl_new_all <- fl_new %>% mutate(latbin=cut(latitude, c(30,33,36,39,42,45,48), labels = c("30-33", "33-36", "36-39", "39-42","42-45", "45-48"))) %>% group_by(latbin) %>% mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm=TRUE)) %>% mutate(difference = mean-mean0513) %>% drop_na(difference) # dropped NA values for plotting fl_new_difference <- fl_new_all %>% group_by(difference) %>% select(latbin, difference) %>% rename("Latitude" = "latbin", "Difference in Flowering Dates" = "difference") # Finding average flowering dates for the recent period (DOYs taken from "mean" column of fl_new_all) origin_date2 <- as.Date(paste0(2025, "-01-01")) fl_new_date1 <- as.Date(93 - 1, origin = origin_date2) fl_new_date2 <- as.Date(94 - 1, origin = origin_date2) fl_new_date3 <- as.Date(96 - 1, origin = origin_date2) fl_new_dates <- c("April 3", "April 3", "April 4", "April 4", "April 6", "April 6") # Selected 1 row for each latitude band difference fl_new_difference <- fl_new_difference[c(1, 1194, 690, 2151, 505, 2810), ] fl_new_difference <- cbind(fl_new_difference, fl_new_dates) fl_new_difference <- fl_new_difference %>% rename("Flowering Date" = "...3") ``` ## 7. ### Repeat Process for Ruby-throated Hummingbirds - Used data from eBird and Journey North in addition to iNaturalist and the US NPN. My eBird datasets can be found on figshare here: - 1995-2021: - 2022-2025: Visit each link and click "download" Or: Download the Ruby-throated Hummingbird data from eBird by visiting: , filter by year Since these flowers are spring ephemerals, warmer winter temperatures, or more extreme heat in spring and summer, may cause this trend, as these flowers will not bloom under extreme heat, or until they have gone through a period of sufficient cooling [@kudo2019]. Additionally, the average first observation date for Ruby-throated hummingbirds has been generally shifting earlier with increasing latitudes. Between latitudes 30 and 36, though, Ruby-throats have been sighted later on average compared to the early period. This may be due to longer overwintering periods [@courter2013]. These trends do somewhat align, especially at higher latitudes. So, Red Columbine and Red Buckeye should be available when Ruby-throats migrate back to higher latitudes earlier. But, Ruby-throats may may miss the flowering of these plants at lower latitudes. It is important to note that this dataset is relatively small, and data used to acquire average arrival/flowering dates for 2005 to 2013 was sparse. Additionally, since this data is collected from citizen science projects, the data distribution may not be even. As shown in the observation heatmaps, sightings do tend to be concentrated in urban areas. ## Future Studies In the future, more data could be integrated into this code to create a longer-term understanding of these trends, especially weather data. Additionally, it is important to understand what other Ruby-throat food sources are being affected not only during spring migration, but also during breeding season, fall migration, and overwintering periods. Looking at more geographically accurate boundaries as shown in Courter et al.'s work would also help give more insight into these trends. Understanding trends like these can give insight into how climate change is affecting biodiversity and hopefully help motivate change and showcase why this biodiversity is important to protect. markdown.srcMarkdownNoYaml: # Introduction With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, migrating birds are starting to move back to their breeding grounds earlier each year [@gill2014]. Along with this, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (*Archilochus colubris*), feed on may be changing their flowering times due to climate change [@xie2025]. ![[Ruby-throated Hummingbird]{style="color:darkblue;"}[@ruby-thr2024]](data/rth_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="400"} I want to investigate how the Ruby-throated Hummingbird has been shifting its spring migration patterns at varying latitudes, based on Courter et al., 2013 [@courter2013], and how the appearances of two spring ephemeral species it prefers to feed on during this migration, Red Buckeye (*Aesculus pavia*) and Red Columbine (*Aquilegia canadensis*), has changed (or not changed) over the past 10\* years, also at varying latitudes [@ruby-thra]. \*My maps and graphs are from 2014 to 2025 to account for any incomplete datasets from 2025 ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ![[Red Columbine]{style="color:darkred;"} [@wildcola]](data/cb_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="200"} ![[Red Buckeye]{style="color:darkred;"} [@redbucka]](data/rb_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="226"} ::: I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back to their breeding grounds earlier each year, and that they are arriving at higher latitudes increasingly earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of Red Columbine and Red Buckeye will be earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes compared to previous years. So, as Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate back earlier, these flowers may not be available at lower latitudes for them to feed on. # Materials and Methods ::: panel-tabset ## 1. ### Install Packages and Load Libraries ```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE #install.packages("leaflet") # Dynamic maps #install.packages("leaflet.providers") # Different Basemaps #install.packages("leaflet.extras") # Heatmaps #install.packages("rinat") # Downloads iNaturalist data #install.packages("rnpn") # Downloads US National Phenology Network Data #install.packages("plotly") # Interactive graphs library(doParallel) # Download data in a parallel loop library(foreach) # Download data in a loop library(plotly) library(leaflet) library(leaflet.providers) library(leaflet.extras) library(rinat) library(rnpn) library(knitr) # Making tables library(rvest) # Used to download data from Journey North library(dplyr) # Mutating and filtering data library(lubridate) # Parsing date data library(tidyr) # Cleaning data library(ggplot2)# Plotting trends ``` ## 2. ### Flowers: Load iNaturalist and US NPN Data. - Average Flowering/Arrival Times (2014-2025) ```{r, message=FALSE} #| code-fold: TRUE late_plot <- ggplot() + geom_point(data = fl_new_all, aes(x = mean, y = latitude, color = "Mean"), size = 0.1) + geom_smooth(data = fl_new_all, aes(x = mean, y = latitude, color = "Flowers"), method = "lm") + geom_point(data = rth_new_all, aes(x = mean, y = latitude, color ="Mean"), size = 0.1) + geom_smooth(data = rth_new_all, aes(x = mean, y = latitude, color = "Ruby-throats"), method = "lm") + labs(title = "Average Flowering/Arrival Times (2014-2025)", x = "Mean Arrival/Flower Date (Year Days)", y = "Latitude") + theme(plot.title = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12), axis.title = element_text(family = "serif", size = 10), panel.background = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_line(color = "lightblue"), legend.text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 10), axis.text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 10)) + scale_color_manual(name = "Legend", breaks = c("Mean", "Flowers", "Ruby-throats"), values = c("Mean" = "gray", "Flowers" = "darkred", "Ruby-throats" = "darkblue")) ggplotly(late_plot) ``` Generally, Red Columbine and Red Buckeye flowering happens over a shorter time within Ruby-throat spring migration, and first flowering sightings begin about a week (March 26th for Ruby-throat arrival and April 3rd for flower sightings, as based on the tables of 2014-2025 arrival/flowering times) after Ruby-throat arrival at the lowest latitudes. # Conclusions Trends for Red Columbine and Red Buckeye show that the timing of their first observations have changed from the 2005-2013 average. At the highest latitudes, flowering times are later than the early average. But for latitudes between 30 and 36, flowers have been sighted later than in previous years. Since these flowers are spring ephemerals, warmer winter temperatures, or more extreme heat in spring and summer, may cause this trend, as these flowers will not bloom under extreme heat, or until they have gone through a period of sufficient cooling [@kudo2019]. Additionally, the average first observation date for Ruby-throated hummingbirds has been generally shifting earlier with increasing latitudes. Between latitudes 30 and 36, though, Ruby-throats have been sighted later on average compared to the early period. This may be due to longer overwintering periods [@courter2013]. These trends do somewhat align, especially at higher latitudes. So, Red Columbine and Red Buckeye should be available when Ruby-throats migrate back to higher latitudes earlier. But, Ruby-throats may may miss the flowering of these plants at lower latitudes. It is important to note that this dataset is relatively small, and data used to acquire average arrival/flowering dates for 2005 to 2013 was sparse. Additionally, since this data is collected from citizen science projects, the data distribution may not be even. As shown in the observation heatmaps, sightings do tend to be concentrated in urban areas. ## Future Studies In the future, more data could be integrated into this code to create a longer-term understanding of these trends, especially weather data. Additionally, it is important to understand what other Ruby-throat food sources are being affected not only during spring migration, but also during breeding season, fall migration, and overwintering periods. Looking at more geographically accurate boundaries as shown in Courter et al.'s work would also help give more insight into these trends. Understanding trends like these can give insight into how climate change is affecting biodiversity and hopefully help motivate change and showcase why this biodiversity is important to protect.
